note: The row-parity oracle. Each rule is translated to a WHERE clause and run
against the fixture, and evaluated by SEL over the same rows loaded as a
context. The two id lists must match.
This is the only oracle that exercises the `relation` binding, because a
correlated subquery has nothing to correlate to without a query around it.
The closed corpus in expressions.selo covers everything that does not need
a table; this covers what does.
`expect` is not the answer being asserted -- the answer is whatever SEL
says. It is a guard that the fixture still makes the rule discriminate:
the driver fails if a rule selects every order or none, because a rule that

`correlate.raw` is raw SQL by design -- it is the one place a host says something the map cannot know -- and raw SQL does not travel between dialects. So it is written per dialect here, and the driver picks. Backticks are MySQL-family and SQLite; PostgreSQL wants double quotes.
A rule may also state that a dialect REFUSES it (`refuse`, per dialect),
which rows over a text column SEL itself refuses (`raises`), and -- only for
docs/SQL-KINDS.md section 6's exclusion 4 -- an answer the database is
allowed to give that SEL does not (`database`, with `excluded` saying why).
Refused rows are absent from what SEL selects, so the ordinary comparison is
the warrant: SQL must not report a match for a row SEL would not answer for.
select: SELECT id FROM o WHERE {} ORDER BY id

context.query: SELECT id, credit_limit, code, code AS code_u FROM o ORDER BY id

ITEMS.query: SELECT order_id, qty, price, sku, value FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id, sku

SKUS.query: SELECT order_id, sku FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id, sku

NOTES.query: SELECT order_id, note FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id, sku

rules.name: sku in the line set
rules.note: SKUS projects one column, so SEL reads it as a list of scalars and IN means the same thing on both sides. IN over the multi-field ITEMS is refused; see the refusal case in sql/cases/09-refusals.sqlt.

rules.name: sku matches, wrong case
rules.degenerate: Empty is the point. The fixture's columns are utf8mb4_general_ci, so a server comparing them under the column collation answers [1] and SEL answers []. This rule is the collation carried into a correlated subquery, which nothing else here checks.

rules.name: a NULL among the rows must not swallow a NOT
a NULL inside an ALL body is not a failed row
a NULL matched positively still answers
a text column compared as a number
rules.why: The report this came from, reduced: a VARCHAR column of EAV values compared numerically. MariaDB reads '25/298' as 25 and 'x' and '' as 0, so before the guard this selected orders 1, 2, 3 and 4 -- three of them rows SEL refuses. sqlite cannot ask whether a value is a number -- no REGEXP, and CAST answers 0 for 'abc' rather than saying so -- so it has no numericGuard and the rule is refused rather than emitted unguarded. docs/SQL-KINDS.md section 5.

rules.name: an undeclared column compared as a number
rules.why: The same column with no declared type, which is what an application gets when it does not say. UNKNOWN takes the guard for the same reason TEXT does, and this is the only place that path is measured against a server.

rules.name: arithmetic over a text column
rules.why: Comparison is not the only numeric context. `* 1` is also the workaround docs/SQL-KINDS.md section 4.1a offers for the function-argument family, so this is the rule that says the workaround actually works on a server.

rules.name: the guard inside a correlated subquery
rules.why: ALL needs no exclusion: it refuses on any bad element whatever the order, and NOT EXISTS (... IS NOT TRUE) turns the guard's NULL into FALSE. Orders 1 and 2 hold a non-numeric value and SEL refuses both; order 4 answers FALSE on a numeric 0 without reaching anything bad.

rules.name: ANY over a relation with one bad element
rules.why: docs/SQL-KINDS.md section 6, exclusion 4, made runnable. SEL's ANY short-circuits, so it reaches AB-1000's 'x' first and refuses order 1; SQL's EXISTS has no order and answers TRUE on CD-2000's 9. SEL has no single answer to be faithful to -- the other ordering answers TRUE -- so the warrant holds only in its weakened form. The guard changes nothing here either way, and order 2, whose only element is bad, is excluded by both sides.
rules.excluded: SQL-KINDS.md section 6 exclusion 4: ANY short-circuits and a relation has no order

rules.name: an undeclared column used as a boolean
rules.why: The other half of the warrant, and the half with no guard: no dialect can ask whether a value is a boolean, because in the MySQL family a boolean IS a TINYINT. Every dialect refuses, so no server is reached -- which is the point.

rules.name: the comparison that matched every row
rules.why: The report as written: `T == 0` over a text column. MariaDB casts both 'x' and '' to 0, so this selected orders 3 and 4 -- rows SEL refuses -- and on a table of non-numeric values it selects all of them. It selects nothing now, and nothing is what SEL selects: order 1 is '25' and order 5 is '30', both FALSE, and the other three SEL refuses outright. Declared degenerate because an empty answer is the whole point here, not a fixture that stopped discriminating.
rules.degenerate: selects nothing, and that is the assertion
